name: Microsoft COCO (Common Objects in Context)
description: A large-scale dataset for object detection, segmentation, and captioning containing images of complex everyday scenes with common objects in their natural context. The dataset contains 91 object categories with per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization. Images depict non-iconic views of objects with rich contextual relationships.
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollár, and C. L. Zitnick,
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr using a novel pipeline that queries for pairs of objects in conjunction with scene-based queries to gather non-iconic images containing contextual relationships. The collection strategy involved searching for pairwise combinations of object categories (e.g., 'dog + car') and scene/object category pairs rather than single object categories to avoid iconic images. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. For categories where enough images could not be found, single category searches were performed with explicit filtering to remove iconic images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were harvested from Flickr, a photo-sharing platform containing photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. The collection focused on gathering images depicting complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed using detection methods. Images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across train/validation/test splits. An explicit filtering stage was performed using AMT workers to remove invalid or iconic images from candidate image sets, with workers shown examples of iconic and non-iconic images to guide their decisions.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A three-stage annotation pipeline was employed: (1) Category labeling: 8 workers per image used a hierarchical approach to indicate which of 91 object categories were present, dragging category icons onto one instance of each category. A category was considered present if any worker indicated it. (2) Instance spotting: 8 workers per image placed crosses on up to 10 instances of each labeled category, with magnifying glass functionality for small objects. (3) Instance segmentation: Single workers segmented each object instance using a modified OpenSurfaces interface with zoom functionality. Workers were required to complete a training task for each object category before being allowed to segment instances. Segmentations were then verified by 3-5 workers; segmentations receiving at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were accepted. For images with more than 10 instances of a category, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single segment.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Multiple workers (3 to 5) judged each segmentation to ensure quality. Segmentations of insufficient quality were discarded and corresponding instances added back to the pool. Workers who consistently produced poor segmentations had all their work discarded. The verification stage required 4 of 5 favorable votes for a segmentation to be accepted.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Category labeling: 8 workers per image. Instance spotting: 8 workers per image. Instance segmentation: 1 worker per instance. Segmentation verification: 3-5 workers per segmentation.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is split into two roughly equal parts. The first half was released in 2014 containing 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The cumulative 2015 release will contain a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. The 2014 release is limited to a subset of 80 categories; segmentations for some of the remaining 11 categories may be added in the cumulative 2015 release.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses only on 'thing' categories (objects for which individual instances may be easily labeled) and does not include 'stuff' categories (materials and objects with no clear boundaries like sky, street, grass). The dataset is limited to entry-level categories commonly used by humans when describing objects, excluding fine-grained categories and object-part categories. Some categories were removed due to ambiguity (mirror, window, door, street sign), confusion with other categories (plate with bowl, desk with dining table), too many instances (hat, shoe, eyeglasses), or too few instances (blender, hair brush). The 2014 release contains segmentations for only 80 of the 91 categories.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training and evaluating object detection and segmentation algorithms. It addresses three core research problems: detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects, and precise 2D localization of objects. The dataset can be used for training, testing, and validation of models. Baseline performance analysis is provided using Deformable Parts Model for bounding box and segmentation detection.
